analysis.one_liner: Requires annual bank stress tests to include scenarios for rising and falling interest rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the annual stress tests the Federal Reserve runs on the largest banks. Today those tests use two scenarios: a baseline and a severely adverse one. This bill would require five, adding scenarios built around interest rates going up and interest rates going down. The point is to catch the kind of losses that sank several regional banks in 2023, when rising rates left them holding bonds worth far less than they had paid. The bill died in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers gain the most. If a large bank fails because rising interest rates eroded the value of its bond holdings, losses fall on depositors, the bank insurance fund, and potentially taxpayers, as the 2023 regional bank failures showed. Banks forced to pass tougher stress tests hold bigger cushions against exactly those losses, making failures and their fallout less likely. Regulators also gain a clearer early-warning picture of rate risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors and the bank insurance fund

how_it_helps.text: It requires the Federal Reserve to run two extra stress-test scenarios each year: one testing whether a large bank can absorb losses if interest rates rise, and one if rates fall.
It raises the number of required stress scenarios from two to five for bank holding companies and nonbank financial companies.
The extra scenarios apply to the same annual stress tests used to judge whether these firms have enough capital to survive adverse economic conditions.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks and bank holding companies would pay. Failing the new scenarios would require them to hold more capital, which reduces profits and shareholder payouts and can slightly limit lending. Nonbank financial companies under Fed supervision face the same added tests.

drawbacks.text: Stress tests that turn out worse for a bank lead regulators to require higher capital buffers, and banks hold capital instead of lending it, so stricter scenarios can modestly constrain credit or raise its cost for borrowers.
Adding two more scenarios, including one for rate increases, increases the regulatory testing burden on large banks and the Federal Reserve's own supervisory workload.
Interest-rate risk on securities is already monitored through other supervisory channels, so supporters would have to show the new scenarios add protection beyond what existing exams catch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: banks that survive an interest-rate shock are less likely to fail, which protects depositors and the federal insurance fund. The cost is that banks holding more capital earn less and may lend somewhat less, and testing both rate directions adds to the burden of an already demanding annual exercise. On balance, after 2023's bank failures exposed exactly this gap in stress testing, the safety benefit looks larger than the lending cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2023 and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat untouched until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 9, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further movement after the referral.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks came out ahead: without the added scenarios, stress tests remain easier to pass and capital requirements stay lower than the bill would have allowed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks that avoided tougher tests

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member took a position on the bill — its Democratic sponsor — so the record shows no partisan split either way.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: Stress tests that include interest-rate swings would flag banks that lose value on their bond and loan portfolios when rates move, leading regulators to require bigger capital cushions. That cuts into profits and dividends but leaves the banks and the deposit insurance fund safer, which matters to anyone who keeps money in a bank account.

industries.industry: Nonbank financial companies supervised by the Federal Reserve
industries.note: Nonbank financial firms designated for Federal Reserve supervision would also face the added interest-rate scenarios. The effect is mixed: closer scrutiny and possibly higher capital requirements, but a lower chance of a disorderly failure.
